ideas.idea: The delivery failures reflect the organisation’s policies and system design rather than insufficient developer effort or motivation.
ideas.note: The system produces the workforce performance it is designed to produce.

ideas.idea: The nobody-idle policy exemplifies a Resource Topology that optimises specialist utilisation rather than end-to-end customer delivery.
ideas.note: The primer defines this topology and its utilisation objective.

ideas.idea: Sharing developers across squads fragments attention, creates dependencies and waiting, and reduces effective delivery capacity.
ideas.note: Direct application of the sources’ multitasking and overload mechanisms; no measured percentage is implied.

ideas.idea: Communication overhead can grow non-linearly with team size and reduce total team output.
ideas.note: Jones models communication overhead and peak productive team size, rather than measuring these nine squads.

ideas.idea: Multi-squad communication overhead grows exponentially in this engineering group.
ideas.note: Jones presents conditional team-size models, not an exponential law for cross-squad membership.

ideas.idea: Interruptions increase sequencing errors and impose cognitive recovery costs.
ideas.note: The interruption study directly measures sequencing errors; it does not quantify a software-team capacity loss.

ideas.idea: Time pressure, high workload, distraction and simultaneous tasks make operational errors more likely.
ideas.note: The handbook explicitly lists these error precursors.

ideas.idea: Taking on additional tasks while blocked can leave several tasks active together, hiding progress and preventing colleagues from helping.
ideas.note: The Limit Work in Progress practice describes this exact sequence.

ideas.idea: Carried-over work and delays between planning and execution cause loss of context.
ideas.note: The source names carry-over and critical bug fixes as causes.

ideas.idea: Unfinished work accumulates as a stock that changes subsequent behaviour and can perpetuate overflow.
ideas.note: Accumulation affects system responses; carry-over adds context loss.

ideas.idea: Repeatedly planning above demonstrated delivery capacity is a forecasting failure that creates predictable carry-over.
ideas.note: Forecasts must reflect past performance and current capacity.

ideas.idea: Even a forty per cent improvement from twenty-five points would produce thirty-five points and still miss the forty-point plan.
ideas.note: Correct arithmetic from the question, rather than an idea supplied by a library source.

ideas.idea: Limit work in progress and finish existing work before starting more to improve flow and shorten cycle time.
ideas.note: Includes the equivalent Little’s Law explanation and stop-starting/start-finishing advice.

ideas.idea: Queue delays grow exponentially or approach infinity as human utilisation approaches one hundred per cent.
ideas.note: The sources support overloaded slow flow and Little’s Law, but not this utilisation-dependent mathematical claim.

ideas.idea: One hundred per cent busy people necessarily produce zero or near-zero flow efficiency.
ideas.note: Busy people can coexist with slow flow; the claimed zero-flow limit is not established.

ideas.idea: Optimise and measure work-item flow rather than individual employee utilisation.
ideas.note: Manage Flow explicitly rejects utilisation as the optimisation metric.

ideas.idea: Maintain spare capacity so teams can absorb reviews, tests, incidents and variability without stopping delivery.
ideas.note: The source recommends enough free resources to handle exceptions constructively.

ideas.idea: Engineering should maintain specifically fifteen to twenty per cent operational slack.
ideas.note: Free capacity is supported, but this percentage is not.

ideas.idea: Assign each developer to one dedicated squad and end routine multi-squad allocation.
ideas.note: Direct application of focused work and a cohesive team working towards one objective.

ideas.idea: Reduce the size and complexity of stories and epics, as well as the number being worked on.
ideas.note: Small work batches are distinct from assigning people to one squad.

ideas.idea: Form stable cross-functional teams with the skills and mandate to deliver customer value without cross-unit dependencies.
ideas.note: The Delivery Topology explicitly describes complete cross-functional teams.

ideas.idea: Set squad work-in-progress limits to at most one or two active items per engineer.
ideas.note: The practice asks teams to determine their limit; it supplies no universal one-to-two threshold.

ideas.idea: Cap active work across the engineering group at three epics.
ideas.note: Reducing active epics is supported; three is an added threshold.

ideas.idea: Base sprint plans on recent completed work and current capacity, around twenty-five points in this case.
ideas.note: The question supplies the twenty-five-point baseline.

ideas.idea: Treat the Sprint Backlog as a good-faith forecast and focusing tool rather than a guaranteed scope contract.
ideas.note: The source explicitly warns against firm commitments above historical performance.

ideas.idea: Use overload reduction and single-squad focus as the first intervention because other delivery symptoms depend on that constraint.
ideas.note: Combines the documented multitasking problem with the instruction to focus on the constraining activity.

ideas.idea: Restore psychological safety and trustworthy reporting before reorganising the delivery system.
ideas.note: Reporting and psychological safety are prerequisites for learning from operational information.

ideas.idea: Remove the target and its bonus link as a first step so that capacity and failure information becomes trustworthy.
ideas.note: Measurement pressure and productivity-only rewards distort the signals needed for change.

ideas.idea: Suspend the throughput incentive and reopen the incident review alongside the initial staffing and planning changes.
ideas.note: Aligned system changes remove conflicting incentives and protect reporting.

ideas.idea: The first staffing and planning changes can be made at no cost in the next sprint.
ideas.note: Internal design is controllable; the assertion of no implementation cost is added.

ideas.idea: Leadership should change the no-idle rule because it owns the organisational conditions that produce delivery performance.
ideas.note: Leadership responsibility and internal control support this application.

ideas.idea: No improvement to quality, incentives, incident practice or AI can work until single-squad allocation and WIP controls are in place.
ideas.note: Constraint focus is supported; the categorical failure of every other intervention and strict ordering are not.

ideas.idea: Reduce overload first so progress is visible and later interventions can be assessed against an honest baseline.
ideas.note: WIP control makes status visible and constraint work assumes process measurement.

ideas.idea: Within two or three sprints, carry-over, escaped bugs and incidents will reveal whether dedicated squads worked.
ideas.note: Reviewing and adjusting the experiment is supported; the diagnostic timeframe is added.

ideas.idea: Deduplicating squad assignments will recover twenty to thirty per cent of engineering capacity.
ideas.note: Neither the interruption study nor Kanban quantifies this capacity recovery.

ideas.idea: Context switching consumes twenty to forty per cent of developers’ working day.
ideas.note: The source measures sequencing errors, not a twenty-to-forty-per-cent daily time loss.

ideas.idea: Delivered story points will initially fall when planning becomes honest.
ideas.note: A plausible forecast about changed reporting, not a consequence demonstrated by a source.

ideas.idea: Assess the operating-model change using completed work, carry-over and reliability results rather than inflated point counts.
ideas.note: Flow metrics and iterative review support the measures; the company-specific selection is an application.

ideas.idea: Paying squad leads for story-point throughput encourages point inflation and metric gaming rather than increased customer value.
ideas.note: Goodhart’s observation directly supports this application to a controllable estimate.

ideas.idea: Throughput demands and narrow quantitative rewards displace less visible quality precautions such as testing, reviews and refactoring.
ideas.note: Includes the equivalent efficiency–thoroughness trade-off explanation, rather than counting that mechanism twice.

ideas.idea: Goals viewed as impossible or imposed without acceptance lose their motivating effect.
ideas.note: Difficulty helps only with acceptance and commitment; impossibility undermines motivation.

ideas.idea: Strong commitment to difficult goals can reduce helping colleagues and other organisational citizenship behaviours.
ideas.note: The chapter explicitly reports the decline in citizenship behaviour.

ideas.idea: Individual squad-lead goals can backfire when interdependent teams share the same developers.
ideas.note: The source recommends group goals when employees depend on one another.

ideas.idea: Pay motivates effectively only when trust, accurate performance measurement and credible reward contingencies are present.
ideas.note: The text lists these conditions for effective pay motivation.

ideas.idea: Suspend or remove the link between squad-lead bonuses and raw point throughput.
ideas.note: Direct response to productivity-only incentives and controllable proxy measurements; J does not propose removing the bonus.

ideas.idea: Use shared customer and service outcomes as performance goals rather than raw feature or point volume.
ideas.note: Outcomes are the aim, and rewards should track actual performance.

ideas.idea: Continue using velocity for empirical forecasting rather than individual performance evaluation.
ideas.note: The field guide supports historical forecasting; the Scrum Guide itself does not mandate velocity.

ideas.idea: Use lead time, cycle time and completed customer-value work to assess delivery flow.
ideas.note: The Kanban practice defines all three flow measures.

ideas.idea: Track reliability through escaped defects, change failures or recovery time alongside delivery volume.
ideas.note: The library links delivery-performance measures, monitoring and incident remediation; exact dashboard design is a local application.

ideas.idea: Use Unbroken Customer Flow Time as a replacement performance metric.
ideas.note: No library passage defines or recommends this named metric.

ideas.idea: Review the delivery and reliability dashboard jointly without paying bonuses against its measures.
ideas.note: Uses measurements for understanding work rather than financial control.

ideas.idea: Goal setting and financial incentives can improve performance but conflict with warnings about proxy gaming, neglected quality or damaged motivation.
ideas.note: Both sides of the incentives/goal-setting tension are present in the library.

ideas.idea: Let squads participate in setting challenging, accepted goals on customer outcomes.
ideas.note: Participation increases commitment; OKRs connect team goals to outcomes.

ideas.idea: Change what bonuses measure rather than assuming all bonuses should be abolished.
ideas.note: The incentive guidance asks for performance-linked design, not universal abolition.

ideas.idea: Bonus schemes can motivate performance but can also create jealousy and undermine teamwork.
ideas.note: The Google award example and broader bonus discussion support both sides.

ideas.idea: A reported survey found success with seventy-three per cent of individual and seventy-five per cent of small-group incentive schemes.
ideas.note: A historical survey result, not an estimate for this engineering group.

ideas.idea: Pro-incentive evidence from countable work may not transfer to self-estimated story points.
ideas.note: A reasonable distinction, but the source does not delimit its evidence to countable work or compare it with story points.

ideas.idea: Goal setting can encourage easy targets, unhealthy competition and even sabotage.
ideas.note: These are explicit examples in the goal-theory cautions.

ideas.idea: Deming’s process-improvement emphasis conflicts with goal-setting theory’s focus on reaching numerical accomplishments.
ideas.note: The management text directly contrasts these approaches.

ideas.idea: Stretch goals work for simple independent tasks but systematically induce gaming in complex software work.
ideas.note: The caveats and gaming risk are supported, but this universal simple-versus-complex boundary is not.

ideas.idea: OKR guidance claims a threefold productivity gain while measurement research warns about controlled metrics and weak productivity evidence.
ideas.note: The threefold figure is reported as a vendor claim in the library, not validated for this company.

ideas.idea: More shipped features or points do not necessarily produce better customer outcomes and may simply increase cost.
ideas.note: The primer explicitly distinguishes outputs from outcomes.

ideas.idea: Marketing’s feature target and engineering’s quality work compete for shared capacity, so leadership must explicitly decide the trade-off.
ideas.note: Production and prevention compete; unaddressed goal conflict favours schedule pressure.

ideas.idea: Schedule acceleration adds small increments of risk that can accumulate unnoticed.
ideas.note: The board describes incremental risk acceptance under schedule pressure.

ideas.idea: Engineering shortcuts create technical debt whose interest slows future changes and can destabilise the product.
ideas.note: The technical-debt practice explicitly describes rework, interest and slower, less stable systems.

ideas.idea: Defects and firefighting consume feature capacity, causing more delay and pressure for further shortcuts.
ideas.note: The debt cycle and poor-quality rework premises directly support the reinforcing loop.

ideas.idea: Engineering’s claim that bugs cause this company’s churn is established and the proposed changes will reduce it.
ideas.note: Poor quality can cause dissatisfaction and lost sales; no source establishes the cause of this company’s churn.

ideas.idea: Test whether bugs cause churn rather than accepting either department’s account without customer evidence.
ideas.note: The software text leaves fault tolerance open; cohort analysis supports testing the customer explanation.

ideas.idea: Compare churned accounts with their incident and support-ticket histories.
ideas.note: Customer segmentation and correlating complaints with operational events support this application.

ideas.idea: Customers may tolerate faulty software when its benefits outweigh the faults, so fault count alone does not determine retention.
ideas.note: The software text treats acceptable fault experiences as an economic and customer-value question.

ideas.idea: Poor quality often loses sales, yet software evidence can show only a small average rating difference for faultier dependencies.
ideas.note: The Android study measures ratings, not this SaaS company’s churn.

ideas.idea: Quality and productivity require company-wide ownership rather than assignment to engineering alone.
ideas.note: Leadership conditions and company-wide dedication make quality a shared responsibility.

ideas.idea: Marketing and engineering may classify the same behaviour differently as a bug or a feature.
ideas.note: The text explicitly identifies classifier-dependent fault definitions.

ideas.idea: Agree one shared definition of a defect before interpreting quality measures.
ideas.note: A direct response to the stated ambiguity in fault classification.

ideas.idea: Give Marketing, Product and Engineering one shared customer-outcome or North Star measure.
ideas.note: The North Star connects product work to business outcomes and shared alignment.

ideas.idea: Assign one respected Product Owner per product line to arbitrate feature and defect priorities.
ideas.note: The Product Owner is one person and the organisation must respect their backlog decisions.

ideas.idea: Keep authority to stop unsafe releases separate from management of growth schedules and costs.
ideas.note: The board explicitly separates technical authority from schedule and funding authority.

ideas.idea: Use Weighted Shortest Job First, dividing cost of delay by job size, to prioritise work jointly across departments.
ideas.note: The practice gives the formula and prioritises smaller, cost-beneficial jobs.

ideas.idea: Reserve seventy per cent of capacity for features, twenty per cent for debt and ten per cent for reliability.
ideas.note: The priority matrix supports explicit trade-offs, not this percentage allocation or these categories.

ideas.idea: Some technical debt is a defensible short-term investment if it remains visible, tracked and managed.
ideas.note: The practice explicitly recognises useful debt and the risk of an unmanaged debt cycle.

ideas.idea: Automated tests prevent a queue forming in front of manual testers.
ideas.note: The test-automation practice makes this specific flow argument.

ideas.idea: Fixed deadlines can improve focus and quick problem solving can confer competitive advantage, despite the risks of permanent overload.
ideas.note: These passages support deadlines and speed, with sustainable-pace constraints.

ideas.idea: Manufacturing quality-control ideas may not transfer directly to software, whose finished bits can be copied perfectly.
ideas.note: Jones distinguishes replication quality from software development; the business text credits Deming.

ideas.idea: Human error is a symptom of deeper organisational weaknesses, so stopping an investigation at the last person leaves the system failure unresolved.
ideas.note: Includes the false reassurance created by replacing or retraining the person closest to failure.

ideas.idea: The strength of controls around a human error determines the severity of its consequences.
ideas.note: The handbook distinguishes error frequency from consequence severity.

ideas.idea: Ask why review, tests, release controls or rollback allowed a single merge to become a prolonged outage.
ideas.note: Investigate what could have prevented or mitigated the event, including defences that failed.

ideas.idea: Fear of punishment suppresses near-miss reporting and trust, while psychological safety enables honest incident information and learning.
ideas.note: The reporting and learning consequences are explicit.

ideas.idea: Introduce or reopen a blameless system-focused postmortem that reconstructs the incident and its contributing conditions.
ideas.note: The practice describes this review purpose and approach.

ideas.idea: Pause the developer’s performance plan until a fair systemic investigation has been completed.
ideas.note: The guide requires fuller investigation and relevant tests before formal individual action.

ideas.idea: Rescind the developer’s performance plan outright on the basis that the incident was systemic.
ideas.note: The guide opposes automatic targeting but does not establish this developer’s culpability or require unconditional withdrawal.

ideas.idea: Use the substitution test and a culpability decision tree before deciding whether individual action is justified.
ideas.note: The tools ask whether comparable peers would have acted similarly under the same conditions.

ideas.idea: The substitution test is already certain or almost certain to exonerate this developer.
ideas.note: The test is supported, but no investigation establishes how comparable peers would actually respond.

ideas.idea: Distinguish honest error from reckless or deliberate violations and retain proportionate individual accountability.
ideas.note: Just culture explicitly preserves a route to individual action; context and workable safeguards matter.

ideas.idea: Keep incident learning and disciplinary or personal-accountability processes separate.
ideas.note: The Forest Service guide explicitly requires a firewall.

ideas.idea: Just-culture frameworks differ in how they retain individual intervention, separate personal accountability or prohibit disciplinary use of learning-review evidence.
ideas.note: Systemic learning and personal accountability are not identical across these frameworks.

ideas.idea: DOE’s root-cause approach conflicts with the Forest Service FLA’s rejection of causal statements in favour of context and networked conditions.
ideas.note: The sources explicitly take different positions on root-cause explanation.

ideas.idea: Incident recommendations can add workplace complexity and increase risk, so a long action list is not automatically an improvement.
ideas.note: The guide explicitly warns about recommendation-induced risk.

ideas.idea: Write a shared incident account before selecting a short set of actions with named owners.
ideas.note: The story comes before documentation; retained recommendations need responsibility and dates.

ideas.idea: Keep senior business stakeholders out of the postmortem meeting and involve them after engineers review the draft.
ideas.note: The source gives both the exclusion and the later review point.

ideas.idea: Reconstruct what participants knew and why their actions made sense at the time, while using hindsight carefully to improve future choices.
ideas.note: The sources caution against judging past decisions solely from known outcomes.

ideas.idea: Punishing this developer guarantees that similar outages will recur.
ideas.note: The source warns about persistent risk if latent causes remain; it does not guarantee a particular future outage.

ideas.idea: Over eighty per cent of failures or errors are caused by latent organisational conditions rather than active individual mistakes.
ideas.note: DOE says about 80% of events involve human error, then about 70% of those errors involve organisational weaknesses; it does not give the asserted >80% latent share.

ideas.idea: Pure blameless models assert that all human errors are entirely system-induced and individual discipline is always counterproductive.
ideas.note: The sources do not establish this universal doctrine; the learning-review firewall is narrower.

ideas.idea: Senior managers can miss most frontline problems, making safe employee feedback essential.
ideas.note: The text reports Yoshida’s 4% top-management and 100% employee awareness figures.

ideas.idea: Accountability can mean providing an honest account and holding the organisation responsible for learning and system improvements.
ideas.note: The Forest Service guide explicitly defines accountability this way.

ideas.idea: Improving a non-bottleneck can yield no total throughput benefit or worsen pressure on a downstream constraint.
ideas.note: This includes the conditional warning about generating code faster than review or release can absorb it.

ideas.idea: Apply the constraint cycle: identify the bottleneck, exploit existing capacity, subordinate other work, elevate it and repeat.
ideas.note: The library lists the five stages and the need to find the next bottleneck.

ideas.idea: Map the value stream jointly to find the single largest constraint and establish shared facts across departments.
ideas.note: The mapping practice supplies shared visibility, decision data and one constraint.

ideas.idea: Check how often each process step receives usable work without clarification or rework.
ideas.note: The value-stream mapping quality measure tests hand-off completeness.

ideas.idea: Capping WIP before mapping the constraint departs from the source’s identify-first order but is justified here as a reversible response to visible overload.
ideas.note: The identify-first sequence is documented; the local justification for reversing it is the answer’s judgement.

ideas.idea: Buying tools as a quick fix can divert attention and investment from the underlying organisational solution.
ideas.note: The shifting-the-burden mechanism directly supports this application.

ideas.idea: A short-term output fix can create delayed side effects that worsen the original delivery problem.
ideas.note: Fixes that fail is distinct from diversion of investment in a fundamental solution.

ideas.idea: Code writing is definitively not the company’s bottleneck; review, testing, fragmented attention or release safety are.
ideas.note: The sources support plausible constraints and focus costs but require investigation to establish this company’s actual bottleneck.

ideas.idea: AI-generated code introduced into this system will increase defects and outages.
ideas.note: Downstream overload and AI error costs are supported; a definite increase in defects or outages is not demonstrated.

ideas.idea: AI adoption will double the volume of unverified code entering the pipeline.
ideas.note: More upstream output can overload a constraint, but no source supplies a doubling estimate.

ideas.idea: Vendors promise immediate thirty to forty per cent improvements from AI coding assistants.
ideas.note: No source carries this specific coding-assistant vendor claim; the macroeconomic AI forecast concerns a different measure and timescale.

ideas.idea: Defer broad AI coding-tool adoption until flow and release safety have been stabilised.
ideas.note: Constraint focus and evaluating hidden error costs support this sequencing application.

ideas.idea: Aim AI investment at a named bottleneck rather than generic adoption.
ideas.note: The primer explicitly recommends the specific bottleneck over generic adoption.

ideas.idea: AI can broaden team skills and work mandates, reducing dependence on scarce specialists.
ideas.note: The primer makes this design claim; it is not a measured productivity result.

ideas.idea: AI creates additional human monitoring responsibilities and processes that require real capacity.
ideas.note: The primer explicitly predicts new monitoring work.

ideas.idea: Pilot AI in a bounded team or period, measure before and after, and evaluate its effect on the chosen constraint.
ideas.note: Baseline economic measurement and bottleneck targeting support a bounded local evaluation.

ideas.idea: Compare manual cost with AI access, adaptation, supervision and error-correction costs before investing.
ideas.note: The Westerman framework explicitly supplies this comparison.

ideas.idea: AI’s error-detection and correction cost is especially problematic while reviewers are overloaded and release controls are weak.
ideas.note: A direct application of the supervision cost and documented overload mechanism.

ideas.idea: Redirect AI spending towards automated test generation, regression detection, static analysis and release or pull-request checks.
ideas.note: Targeting constraints and test automation are supported; these specific AI quality-assurance capabilities and their benefits are not established.

ideas.idea: AI optimism about abundant expertise conflicts with the risk of quick fixes, added complexity and error-supervision costs.
ideas.note: Both the optimistic design claims and the countervailing system costs are in the library.

ideas.idea: A macroeconomic forecast of forty per cent AI labour-productivity growth does not establish a forty per cent squad-throughput gain by Q1.
ideas.note: The quoted forecast concerns broad economic effects by 2035 and holistic implementation.

ideas.idea: New organisational changes can initially raise error risk and create new ways for a complex system to fail.
ideas.note: The handbook warns about unintended effects and competition between old and new ways.

ideas.idea: Continuous integration adoption does not automatically increase merged output; one study found slower growth in merged commits afterwards.
ideas.note: The result concerns the rate of increase, not an absolute decline in commits.

ideas.idea: A passing build can conceal ignored failures; one study found them in twelve per cent of passing builds.
ideas.note: The reported study supports the precise figure.

ideas.idea: Treat public productivity benchmarks and vendor tool claims sceptically because they may be marketing rather than meaningful evidence.
ideas.note: The source distinguishes performance and productivity and discusses benchmark marketing.

ideas.idea: Strengthen automated testing and deployment quality gates to prevent unsafe code reaching production.
ideas.note: The library supports pre-release tests and quality gates; K additionally specifies mandatory build stops.

ideas.idea: Resource utilisation and delivery-date optimisation are competing scheduling objectives that leadership must choose between.
ideas.note: The library describes both objectives; this does not establish a universal queueing theorem.

ideas.idea: Classical accounting or scientific management prescribes full human utilisation as the way to maximise labour cost efficiency.
ideas.note: The primer describes a possible utilisation-oriented design, not this universal prescription by classical accounting or management.

ideas.idea: Resource Topology is appropriate for some temporary specialist engagements and is not inherently wrong for every organisation.
ideas.note: The primer explicitly gives the temporary hiring example and fit-for-purpose qualification.

ideas.idea: Fixed sprint timeboxes and continuous Kanban pull differ over batching and when ready work should be released.
ideas.note: Scrum uses fixed Sprints; Kanban supports deploying ready items without waiting for a batch.

ideas.idea: Scrum requires fixed scope commitments, in contrast to Kanban’s adaptive flow.
ideas.note: Timeboxes are fixed, but the guides describe a forecast and scope flexibility; this characterisation overstates the conflict.

ideas.idea: Kanban’s start-where-you-are approach differs from Org Topologies’ insistence on aligning the surrounding organisational design.
ideas.note: The sources differ on the emphasis and scale of structural intervention.

ideas.idea: If dedicated squads do not remove the dependencies, redesign the broader nine-squad and three-product-line structure next.
ideas.note: The primer warns against isolating team improvements from the structures around them.

ideas.idea: Use system archetypes as hypotheses to test with teams rather than labels that erase what is specific to the situation.
ideas.note: The source explicitly warns against prescriptive use of archetypes.

ideas.idea: Engineers need to own the redesign of their work, which requires a safe environment for participation.
ideas.note: Ownership of change and psychological safety are explicit premises.

ideas.idea: Extrinsic financial rewards can diminish intrinsic motivation, even when they increase effort towards a rewarded goal.
ideas.note: Self-determination theory supplies the mechanism, distinct from manipulating a reported metric.

ideas.idea: Unit-level incentive schemes can improve a work area’s results while harming overall company performance.
ideas.note: Gain sharing and misaligned managerial incentives illustrate local gain at corporate expense.

ideas.idea: An output-oriented organisation can create feature bloat without solving the underlying customer problem.
ideas.note: The primer explicitly warns that more delivery need not solve the problem.

ideas.idea: Aggressive schedules can be healthy, provided leadership monitors their effects on safety rather than treating every deadline as inviolable.
ideas.note: The board qualifies rather than universally rejects demanding schedules.

ideas.idea: Estimate developer productivity only after accounting for effort across all relevant development activities.
ideas.note: The text warns against estimating productivity from one isolated activity.

ideas.idea: Demanding faster feature output and fewer bugs is an unresolvable trade-off unless workload constraints are reduced.
ideas.note: ETTO supports competing demands, but not the categorical impossibility of improving both through other system changes.

ideas.idea: Individual performance-and-reward frameworks place responsibility on workers, while system-safety approaches emphasise management’s responsibility for working conditions.
ideas.note: The tension is between emphases, not proof that either school rejects all responsibility at the other level.

ideas.idea: Choose reversible initial interventions so the organisation can learn before committing to a larger redesign.
ideas.note: The primer recommends gradual experimentation and feedback; the local staffing or target choices are applications.

ideas.idea: Withdraw the imposed forty per cent throughput target itself, as well as removing its bonus link.
ideas.note: Withdrawing an unsupported scope target is distinct from merely decoupling pay.

ideas.idea: Offer Marketing a predictable cadence of completed features based on demonstrated capacity instead of promising one feature every week.
ideas.note: Empirical capacity-based forecasting applies to external commitments as well as sprint selection.

ideas.idea: Larger or less cognitively clear changes make peer code review more difficult.
ideas.note: The library covers review work and patch studies, but the cited WebKit passage does not establish the claimed size-and-clarity relationship.

ideas.idea: Flooding review queues with AI-generated code will increase false-positive defect reports.
ideas.note: The library discusses static-analysis false positives, but no passage connects AI-generated review volume to their rate.

ideas.idea: Developer payroll is a variable expense for purposes of the full-utilisation argument.
ideas.note: No source establishes this cost classification for the company’s salaried engineering headcount.

ideas.idea: Use Change Failure Rate as a named replacement for point-velocity performance metrics.
ideas.note: The library discusses delivery-performance metrics and monitoring failures, but does not define or name Change Failure Rate in the converted text.
